metadata.title: Does greater community involvement mean more parent-teacher interaction? Evidence from seven developing countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA-D 2015 microdata for seven countries and constructs school-level aggregates (e.g., the school mean of teacher meeting-demand indicators) that are then merged with student-level predictors. The author states that the school mean of teacher-level variables is calculated using school weights provided in PISA-D, and that final student survey weights are used to estimate the regression models. The dependent variable is a bounded proportion (percentage of teachers receiving parent meeting requests), and the models include robust standard errors; the paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Missing values in independent variables are handled via imputation, with additional missingness indicators included in the regressions to prevent imputed values from driving results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not report a plausible-values (PV) workflow because the analysis is not framed as PV-based achievement modeling; instead, it uses a continuous maths achievement score as a control and focuses on a non-PV outcome (parent-teacher meeting demand as a teacher-reported proportion). Missing-data handling is described as imputation of independent variables, but the paper does not specify the exact imputation algorithm or number of imputations, so the precise missing-data procedure cannot be fully audited from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA-D 2015 data for seven low- and lower-middle-income countries (Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Cambodia, Senegal, Zambia). The target population is approximately 15-year-olds (mostly lower-secondary grades 7–10, plus ~11% upper-secondary) as captured in PISA-D. The outcome is teacher-reported parent demand for personal meetings about students’ progress, converted to a school-level proportion (percentage of teachers receiving meeting requests) and merged with student-level predictors. Teacher-level variables are aggregated to the school level using PISA-D school weights; student-level models are estimated with final student survey weights. Independent variables with missing values are imputed, and the regressions include dummies indicating whether each variable was imputed.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA-D 2015 (15-year-olds), seven countries; outcome from teacher questionnaire (meeting demand proportion)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-by-country OLS coefficients with robust standard errors; no ML metrics reported (no predictive model). Key reported results: community involvement coefficients are non-significant in all countries in the no-control model; instructional resources significant in most countries when ownership is excluded; after adding ownership, instructional resources becomes non-significant in six of seven countries and ownership becomes significant in six of seven countries (except Guatemala). Interaction: SES does not significantly moderate ownership in any country; SES moderates the resources effect in Guatemala, Honduras, and Senegal.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2015 data from Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Cambodia, Senegal, and Zambia, the study leveraged community involvement level, instructional resources, school ownership, and student SES (plus controls) to model parent-teacher meeting demand (percentage of teachers receiving meeting requests), finding that community involvement is largely non-significant while school ownership (private/public) strongly predicts meeting demand in six of seven countries and instructional resources show a mediating pattern through ownership. This indicates that SBM-style community involvement alone may not increase parent-teacher interaction unless paired with school-level resource and governance conditions that enable parents—especially in fee-paying/private settings—to engage teachers, though the study is correlational and cannot establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA-D 2015 data for seven low- and lower-middle-income countries (Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Cambodia, Senegal, Zambia) to examine whether school-based management community involvement is associated with parent-teacher interaction. The outcome is teacher-reported parent demand for personal meetings about students’ progress, converted to a school-level proportion (percentage of teachers receiving requests) and analyzed with country-specific OLS regressions (robust standard errors), with GLM logit models as robustness checks. Across models, community involvement is not significant in most specifications, while school ownership (private vs public) is significant in six of seven countries; instructional resources are significant when ownership is excluded but largely lose significance once ownership is included, consistent with mediation. SES does not moderate the ownership effect, but it moderates the resources effect in Guatemala, Honduras, and Senegal. The analysis is observational and relies on imputation for missing independent variables; the paper does not provide PV-handling details because the focus is on a non-PV outcome.
